claim: R3 reports that serving is shifting from short conversations to long-context applications such as retrieval-augmented generation, long-document question answering, and agent reasoning.
quote: Large language model (LLM) serving is gradually shifting from short conversations to long-context applications such as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) (Lewis et al., 2020), long-document question answering (Bai et al., 2024), and agent reasoning (Yao et al., 2023).

claim: The same source says that prefill must process the entire context and that its computational cost grows rapidly with input length.
quote: Prefill must process the entire context, and its computational cost grows rapidly with input length.

claim: R7 adds that a transformer's KV representation of a token is a function of its entire prefix, so exact reuse is confined to contexts that share a prefix verbatim.
quote: But a transformer's KV representation of a token is a function of its entire prefix, so exact reuse is confined to contexts that share a prefix verbatim.

claim: R18 describes repository-level software engineering as one of the long-running tasks for which LLM agents are increasingly used.
quote: LLM agents are increasingly used for long-running tasks such as repository-level software engineering [Jimenez et al., 2024, Yang et al., 2024] and deep research over the open web [Zheng et al., 2025, Wei et al., 2025].

claim: R18 states that, as agent trajectories grow, session history accumulates continuously while each model invocation operates over a bounded context window, and identifies context management as a central challenge for the agent harness.
quote: As trajectories grow, a central challenge for the agent harness is context management: session history accumulates continuously, while each model invocation operates over a bounded context window.

claim: The first, Recursive Language Models, is described by its authors as a general inference paradigm that treats long prompts as part of an external environment.
quote: We propose Recursive Language Models (RLMs), a general inference paradigm that treats long prompts as part of an external environment and allows the LLM to programmatically examine, decompose, and recursively call itself over snippets of the prompt.

claim: The RLM authors report that it handles inputs up to two orders of magnitude beyond model context windows.
quote: We find that RLMs can successfully process inputs up to two orders of magnitude beyond model context windows and, even for shorter prompts, dramatically outperform the quality of vanilla frontier LLMs and common long-context and coding scaffolds

claim: R17 reports that CLMs achieve 11.4% higher accuracy with 21.5% fewer prefix-reuse FLOPs than the strongest baseline on BrowseComp-Plus, and match its accuracy on TerminalBench 2.1 with 29.5% fewer FLOPs.
quote: Compared with existing harness-defined and action-based methods, CLM achieves 11.4% higher accuracy with 21.5% fewer prefix-reuse FLOPs than the strongest baseline on the deep-research benchmark BrowseComp-Plus (Chen et al., 2025), while matching the strongest baseline's accuracy on the terminal-coding benchmark TerminalBench 2.1 (Merrill et al., 2026) with 29.5% fewer FLOPs.

claim: R17 reports co-designing Suffix Cache Reuse for CLM serving, which it says further reduces server-side compute by 35% relative to standard SGLang at matched performance.
quote: we co-design Suffix Cache Reuse for CLM serving, further reducing server-side compute by 35% relative to standard SGLang at matched performance.

claim: R17 includes recursive language models among the baselines it compares against, on a shared Mini-SWE-Agent backbone.
quote: We compare CLMs against MEM1 (Zhou et al., 2026), Self-Compact (Li et al., 2026b), ACM (Li et al., 2026c), and recursive language models (RLM) (Zhang et al., 2025a) with a shared Mini-SWE-Agent backbone (Merrill et al., 2026).
locator: sec. Coding and Deep Research Tasks, para 23

claim: The original RLM paper frames the approach as an inference paradigm over long prompts held outside the model.
quote: We propose Recursive Language Models (RLMs), a general inference paradigm that treats long prompts as part of an external environment and allows the LLM to programmatically examine, decompose, and recursively call itself over snippets of the prompt.

claim: A reproduction study examined recursion depth, which the original work left at one.
quote: While the original paper relies on a default recursion depth of 1 and suggests deeper recursion as a future direction, this study specifically investigates the impact of scaling the recursion depth.

claim: The reproduction reports that deeper recursion or use on simple retrieval hurts performance and inflates time and tokens.
quote: While depth-1 RLMs effectively boost accuracy on complex reasoning tasks, applying deeper recursion (depth=2) or using RLMs on simple retrieval tasks paradoxically degrades performance and exponentially inflates execution time (e.g., from 3.6s to 344.5s) and token costs.

claim: RLM-Extended addresses deployment gaps in the reference implementations, including local backends.
quote: While the RLM framework introduced by Zhang et al. showed strong performance on long-context tasks, existing reference implementations have practical limitations in termination, reproducibility, and deployment. This paper introduces RLM-Extended, a systems-oriented extension of Recursive Language Models that enforces deterministic termination via an explicit answer variable, immutable context semantics to prevent unintended prompt mutation, and local LLM backend support through an Ollama-based interface.

claim: Context Language Models (CLMs) are described by their authors as implemented by treating the context as a file and allowing the model to make unrestricted updates to that file.
quote: We implement this by treating the context as a file and allowing the model to make unrestricted updates to this file.

claim: The CLM paper compares CLMs against MEM1, Self-Compact, ACM, and recursive language models (RLM) with a shared Mini-SWE-Agent backbone.
quote: We compare CLMs against MEM1 (Zhou et al., 2026), Self-Compact (Li et al., 2026b), ACM (Li et al., 2026c), and recursive language models (RLM) (Zhang et al., 2025a) with a shared Mini-SWE-Agent backbone (Merrill et al., 2026).
locator: sec. Coding and Deep Research Tasks, para 23

claim: The CLM authors report that their Suffix Cache Reuse for CLM serving reduces server-side compute by 35% relative to standard SGLang at matched performance.
quote: we co-design Suffix Cache Reuse for CLM serving, further reducing server-side compute by 35% relative to standard SGLang at matched performance.

claim: The CLM paper introduces Context Language Models as a way for models to manage their own context.
quote: We introduce Context Language Models (CLMs), language models that natively manage their own context.

claim: The CLM authors implement this by treating the context as a file that the model may update without restriction.
quote: We implement this by treating the context as a file and allowing the model to make unrestricted updates to this file.

claim: The coding comparison uses a shared Mini-SWE-Agent backbone and includes recursive language models among the baselines.
quote: We compare CLMs against MEM1 (Zhou et al., 2026), Self-Compact (Li et al., 2026b), ACM (Li et al., 2026c), and recursive language models (RLM) (Zhang et al., 2025a) with a shared Mini-SWE-Agent backbone (Merrill et al., 2026).
locator: sec. Coding and Deep Research Tasks, para 23

claim: On terminal coding, the CLM authors report that CLM matches the strongest baseline's accuracy on TerminalBench 2.1 with fewer FLOPs.
quote: while matching the strongest baseline's accuracy on the terminal-coding benchmark TerminalBench 2.1 (Merrill et al., 2026) with 29.5% fewer FLOPs.

claim: In Suffix Cache Reuse, after an edit replaces a block, the cached states of all surviving tokens are reused and only the newly inserted or appended tokens are reprefilled.
quote: SCR reuses the cached states of all surviving tokens, including 𝐶 , and only reprefills the newly inserted or appended tokens 𝐵 ′ .
locator: sec. (More) Efficient CLM Serving with Suffix Cache Reuse, para 21

claim: Standard prefix-cache reuse, by contrast, must re-prefill everything after the first mismatch.
quote: By contrast, standard prefix-cache reuse must re-prefill all tokens after the first mismatch ( 𝐵 ′ and 𝐶 ).
locator: sec. (More) Efficient CLM Serving with Suffix Cache Reuse, para 21

claim: The CLM authors report that SCR cuts server-side compute by 35% against standard SGLang at matched performance.
quote: Finally, we co-design Suffix Cache Reuse for CLM serving, further reducing server-side compute by 35% relative to standard SGLang at matched performance.

claim: The CLM paper retains stale cache states for surviving suffix tokens, and its authors say this can even be beneficial in some cases.
quote: Surviving suffix tokens 𝐶 thus retain stale cache states that encode the previous prefix, which can even be beneficial in some cases, as it retains richer information from the past.
locator: sec. (More) Efficient CLM Serving with Suffix Cache Reuse, para 21

claim: The Context Language Models paper introduces Suffix Cache Reuse, in which an edit replacing B with B′ reuses the cached states of all surviving tokens and re-prefills only the newly inserted or appended tokens.
quote: We introduce Suffix Cache Reuse (SCR). As shown in Figure 4, when 𝐵 is replaced by 𝐵 ′ after an edit, SCR reuses the cached states of all surviving tokens, including 𝐶 , and only reprefills the newly inserted or appended tokens 𝐵 ′ .
locator: sec. (More) Efficient CLM Serving with Suffix Cache Reuse, para 21

claim: The Context Language Models authors state that standard prefix-cache reuse must re-prefill all tokens after the first mismatch.
quote: By contrast, standard prefix-cache reuse must re-prefill all tokens after the first mismatch ( 𝐵 ′ and 𝐶 ).
locator: sec. (More) Efficient CLM Serving with Suffix Cache Reuse, para 21

claim: Surviving suffix tokens under Suffix Cache Reuse keep stale states that encode the previous prefix, which the authors say can sometimes be beneficial.
quote: Surviving suffix tokens 𝐶 thus retain stale cache states that encode the previous prefix, which can even be beneficial in some cases, as it retains richer information from the past.
locator: sec. (More) Efficient CLM Serving with Suffix Cache Reuse, para 21

claim: Leyline reports that production agentic harnesses fall back to re-prefill on every edit, paying full prefix-recomputation cost.
quote: Production agentic harnesses fall back to re-prefill on every edit, paying full prefix-recomputation cost; kernel-level eviction methods make their own decisions and cannot accept policy directives from outside the kernel.

claim: Leyline's splice kernel lifts replay cache-hit by 11.2 points and cuts latency by up to 241 ms.
quote: The splice kernel lifts replay cache-hit by +11.2 pp and cuts latency by up to 241 ms.

claim: The CacheTune authors note that directly reusing KV cache in non-prefix settings breaks cross-chunk attention and significantly degrades generation quality.
quote: KV Cache reuse offers a direct path to reduce redundant prefill, yet traditional prefix caching applies only to strict-prefix scenarios; directly reusing KV Cache in non-prefix settings breaks the cross-chunk global attention relationships and causes significant degradation in generation quality.

claim: SMem reports that deletion beats suffix recomputation by 8.5x at 512 blocks and 452x at 4096 blocks, which the authors describe as 32-256x the trained length and as probing the cost model rather than a served regime.
quote: deletion beats suffix recomputation by 8.5$\times$ at 512 blocks and 452$\times$ at 4096 blocks (32-256$\times$ the trained length, probing the cost model rather than a served regime)

claim: The Context Language Models paper reports that CLMs, applied zero-shot, achieve 11.4% higher accuracy with 21.5% fewer prefix-reuse FLOPs than the strongest baseline on BrowseComp-Plus.
quote: Compared with existing harness-defined and action-based methods, CLM achieves 11.4% higher accuracy with 21.5% fewer prefix-reuse FLOPs than the strongest baseline on the deep-research benchmark BrowseComp-Plus (Chen et al., 2025), while matching the strongest baseline's accuracy on the terminal-coding benchmark TerminalBench 2.1 (Merrill et al., 2026) with 29.5% fewer FLOPs.

claim: The same paper describes how CLMs can learn context-management strategies through reinforcement learning and internalize them in model weights.
quote: CLMs can also learn context-management strategies through reinforcement learning and internalize them in model weights.
locator: sec. In-Context Learning and Reinforcement Learning for CLMs, para 17

claim: The CAT paper reports that SWE-Compressor reaches a 57.6% solved rate on SWE-Bench-Verified.
quote: On the challenging SWE-Bench-Verified benchmark, SWE-Compressor achieves a 57.6% solved rate, reaching state-of-the-art performance under the setting of agent post-training on a 32B model.

claim: The CAT authors also report that, under a 150-step budget, CAT maintains competitive performance and uses the fewest tokens across all methods.
quote: Under a smaller interaction budget (150 steps), CAT both maintains competitive performance and uses the fewest tokens across all methods.
locator: sec. Context Comparison between CAT and ReAct., para 46

claim: The ACM paper reports that its dual-constraint pipeline improves Qwen3.5-9B over the ReAct baseline by 8% on SWE-Bench Verified.
quote: Using this dual-constraint pipeline, we improve Qwen3.5-9B's search and coding performance over the ReAct baseline by 27% on BrowseComp-Plus (Chen et al., 2025), 16% on DeepSearchQA (Gupta et al., 2026), and 8% on SWE-Bench Verified (Jimenez et al., 2024).

claim: The Focus study evaluated only N=5 SWE-bench Lite instances and reported a 22.7% token reduction with identical accuracy of 3/5 for both agents.
quote: Using an optimized scaffold matching industry best practices (persistent bash + string-replacement editor), we evaluated Focus on N=5 context-intensive instances from SWE-bench Lite using Claude Haiku 4.5. With aggressive prompting that encourages frequent compression, Focus achieves 22.7% token reduction (14.9M ->11.5M tokens) while maintaining identical accuracy (3/5 = 60% for both agents).

claim: The Scroll paper frames context management as a programming task, one that inherits the improving coding abilities of LLMs.
quote: Context management thus becomes a programming task that inherits the improving coding abilities of LLMs

claim: The CLM authors report that, on TerminalBench 2.1, CLM matches the strongest baseline's accuracy with 29.5% fewer FLOPs.
quote: while matching the strongest baseline's accuracy on the terminal-coding benchmark TerminalBench 2.1 (Merrill et al., 2026) with 29.5% fewer FLOPs

claim: The CLM authors also report that Suffix Cache Reuse reduces server-side compute by 35% with matched performance compared with standard SGLang serving.
quote: Finally, we co-design Suffix Cache Reuse for CLM serving, further reducing server-side compute by 35% relative to standard SGLang at matched performance.

claim: Long Code Arena provides six benchmarks for code processing tasks that require project-wide context.
quote: With this work, we aim to close this gap by introducing Long Code Arena, a suite of six benchmarks for code processing tasks that require project-wide context.

claim: SWE-Bench-CL organizes GitHub issues into chronologically ordered sequences to evaluate whether an agent can accumulate experience and transfer knowledge across tasks.
quote: By organizing GitHub issues into chronologically ordered sequences that reflect natural repository evolution, SWE-Bench-CL enables direct evaluation of an agent's ability to accumulate experience, transfer knowledge across tasks, and resist catastrophic forgetting.

claim: Long Code Arena's authors warn that reliance on open-source data can lead to contamination that skews evaluation results.
quote: On the other hand, modern LLMs use most available open-source data for training, and such reliance can lead to data contamination, which in turn can skew the evaluation results.
locator: sec. Limitations and Future Work, para 53

claim: The Recursive Language Models paper proposes RLMs as an inference paradigm that treats long prompts as part of an external environment and lets the model examine, decompose and recursively call itself over snippets.
quote: We propose Recursive Language Models (RLMs), a general inference paradigm that treats long prompts as part of an external environment and allows the LLM to programmatically examine, decompose, and recursively call itself over snippets of the prompt.

claim: The RLM authors report that it outperforms compaction, CodeAct with sub-calls and Claude Code across four long-context tasks while having comparable cost.
quote: We find that RLMs can successfully process inputs up to two orders of magnitude beyond model context windows and, even for shorter prompts, dramatically outperform the quality of vanilla frontier LLMs and common long-context and coding scaffolds (e.g., on GPT-5 by a median across the evaluated benchmarks of $26\%$ against compaction, $130\%$ against CodeAct with sub-calls, and $13\%$ against Claude Code) across four diverse long-context tasks while having comparable cost.

claim: The Context Language Models authors state that cache-reuse gains largely saturate by much shorter prefix.
quote: Performance is robust across 𝐾, while cache-reuse gains largely saturate by much shorter prefix.
locator: sec. B Suffix Cache Reuse, para 55

claim: The Leyline authors state that production agentic harnesses fall back to re-prefill on every edit, paying full prefix-recomputation cost.
quote: Production agentic harnesses fall back to re-prefill on every edit, paying full prefix-recomputation cost; kernel-level eviction methods make their own decisions and cannot accept policy directives from outside the kernel.

claim: The Leyline authors report that their splice kernel lifts replay cache-hit by 11.2 percentage points and cuts latency by up to 241 ms.
quote: The splice kernel lifts replay cache-hit by +11.2 pp and cuts latency by up to 241 ms.

claim: The Scroll paper reports token counts rather than latency or dollar cost, because both depend on serving configuration.
quote: We report token counts rather than latency or dollar cost, as both depend on serving configuration.

claim: The Prompt Cache authors report TTFT reductions of 20× to 70× for CPU inference on LongBench.
quote: In our evaluation, Prompt Cache reduces time-to-first-token (TTFT) latency from 1.5× to 10× for GPU inference with prompt modules on GPU memory and from 20× to 70× for CPU inference, all without any significant accuracy loss.
